FOREWORD This Indian Standard was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards, after the draft finalized by the Ceramicware Sectional Committee had been approved by the Chemical Division Council. Calcite, the essential mineral in limestone is a naturally occurring calcium carbonate having formula CaCOl, consisting of 56.03 percent CaO and 43.97 percent C02. It is normally white in colour and soft, the hardness being only 3 in Mohr's scale. In pottery, calcite is used in glazes. It is used in the manufacture of silica refractories as mineralizer. In glass industry, it is one of the major raw materials used to introduce CaO in a soda-lime-silica glass. Calcium oxide increases the mechanical hardness and tensile str-ength of glass and glaze and improves its durability to acids and to water. In a glaze with a baianced composition, an increase in calcium oxide can reduce the coefficient of thermal expansion. This standard contains 4.2, 4.3 and 5.1 which provide for agreement between the purchaser and the supplier, `1'hecomposition of the Committee responsible for formulation of this standard is given in Annex D.

For- the purpose of deciding whether a particular requirement of this standard is complied with, the final value, observed or calculated, expressing the result of a test or analysis, shall be rounded off in accordance with IS 2:1960 `Rules for rounding off numerical values (revised)'. The number of significant places retained in the rounded off value should be the same as that of the specified value in this standard.

B-3 DETERMINATION CARBONATE B-3.1 Proc~dure B-3.1.1 Dried sample of calcite is taken and weigh 0.5 g in a watch glass. Transfer the sample to 500 ml beaker in which 50 ml (1 :1) HC1 is added. Add 50 ml distilled water and boil the solution gently to expel C02. Then add about 0.5 g of pure NHdCl and 2 drops of methyl-red indicator. Heat the contents of beaker to boiling. Add slowly hot aqueous solution of 4 g ammonium oxalate. Then add dilute ammonia solution drop-wise till the colour of solution becomes just yellowish. Allow the precipitate to stand for 1 h. Test the supernatant liquid for complete precipitation with a drop of ammonium oxalate. B-3.1.2 Filter off the clean supernatant liquid through Whatman No. 42 filter paper fixed in a funnel. Wash the precipitate 2-3 times by recantation with 0.2 percent cold solution of ammonium oxalate. Transfer the precipitate to the filter cone and wash it with cold dilute ammonium oxalate solution until the filtrate is free from chloride ions (test with dilute HNO~ and AgNO~ solution). Allow the liquid to drain off. B-3.1.3 Dry the precipitate by placing the funnel in an air oven at 120�C or on a drying cone. Fold the filter paper to enclose the entire precipitate. Place this packet in a weighed silica crucible. Ignite the paper by gentle heating and then heat the crucible strongly over a burner flame for about 30 min. Cool the crucible first in air and then in a dessicator to room temperature and weigh it quickly. Repeat the process of heating, cooling and weighing until a constant weight is obtained. B-3.2 Calculation Calcium carbonate (as CaCO,), percent by mass = (A -B) x % OF CALCIUM where A = mass in g of crucible and CaO residue, in g; and B = mass of empty crucible, in g. B-4 DETERMINATION OF IMPURITY IN HYDROCHLORIC B-4.1 Procedure INSOLUBLE ACID

Dry the filter paper in a dryer and ignite it in a dried and weighed silica crucible first at low flame and then raised the temperature for 30 min. Cool it in a dessicator and calculate the percent insoluble impurity.

W, = initial weight of crucible with material, and Wj = final weight of crucible with material. B-5 DETERMINATION OF IRON OXIDE

B-5.1 Outline of the Method The orange-red complex produced in acid solution of the sample (pH 4 to 6) by the addition of o-phenanthroline is determined photometrically at approximately 510 nm. B-5.2 Reagents B-5.2.1 Tartaric Acid Solution -- 10 percent (m/v).

B-5.2.2 Hydroxylarnine Hydrochloride Solution -- Dissolve 1 g of the reagent in water. Transfer the solution to a 100-ml volumetric flask, dilute to the mark and mix well. B-5.2.3 Ortho-Phenanthroline Solution -- Dissolve 1 g ofo-phenanthroline monohydrate in 90 ml of water with gentle heating and constant stirring. Cool and dilute to 100 ml. B-5.2.4 Acetate Buffer -- Dissolve 21.5 g of the sodium acetate (C H~COONa, 3 H20) in 300 ml of water containing 2 ml of glacial acetic acid and dilute to 1000 ml. B-5.2.5 Stundard Iron Solution -- Dissolve 0.2 g of pure iron in concentrated hydrochloric acid. Dilute the solution to about 100 ml. Transfer to a 1 000 ml

IS 15751:2007 volumetric flask, dilute to the mark and mix well. Dilute 100 ml of this solution to 1000 ml in a volumetric flask. One millilitre of this diluted solution is equivalent to 0.02 mg of iron (as Fe). B-5.3 Procedure B-5.4 Calculation Ferric oxide as (as Fe,03), percent by mass = #x

B-5.3.1 Solution of the Sample -- Weigh accurately about 2 g of the tinely ground test sample (see 6.2) in a platinum dish. Moisten the sample with 5 ml of water. Add 3 ml of dilute sulphuric acid and 20 ml of hydrofluoric acid and evaporate slowly to dryness on the sand bath or hot plate in a fime cupboard, taking care to avoid spurting. Repeat the process with 10 fill ofhydrofluoric acid. Cool, add 2 ml of dilute sulphuric acid and evaporate as before. Heat the dry residue cautiously until fumes of sulphur trioxide cease to be evolved. Raise the temperature to 1 000"C and ignite for 5 min. Cool and fuse the residue with 1 g of sodium carbonate and dissolve in hydrochloric acid, cool and dilute to 250 ml in a volumetric flask. B.5.3.2 Transfer a 5 ml aliquot of the solution prepared in B-5.3,1 to a 100 ml volumetric flask. Also transfer O, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 ml each of the standard iron solution to seven separate 100 ml volumetric flasks. Then add to each flask 2 ml of tartaric acid solution followed by 2 ml of hydroxylamine hydrochloride solution. Stir well and add 5 ml of o-phenanthroline solution and 10 ml of acetate buffer solution. Allow to stand for 15 min and dilute up to the mark with water. B-5.3.3 Starting with the blank (O ml) solution transfer a suitable portion of the coloured solution, one at a time, to an absorption cell; record the photometric readings using the light band centred approximately at 510 nm, prepare the calibration curve from these readings against concentration of iron (as Fe). Take about so g of the material in China dish and heat to constant weight at 105 + 2�C. Cool it in a desiccator and keep for subsequent tests. II-6.2 Heat 1 g of the above dried material in a platinum crucible in a muffle furnace at 1 000 + 50"C. Cool the crucible and put the contents in a desiccator to constant mass. The loss in mass denotes loss on ignition and the percent loss Inay be calculated. B-7 DETERMINATION OF FREE IRON

Soak about 100 g of the sample in excess of water in a plastic beaker. Mix the sample with a glass rod by vigorously shaking so as to prevent any settlement. Dip a bar magnet into the slurry and gently rotate it in the slurry, 4 to 5 times. Place the magnet on a clean paper and dry at room temperature. Collect the iron filings on the paper. Weigh the filings using electronic balance and note the value. The value is directly taken as percent free iron.
